title: What is global market research and how does it work?
summary: Learn what global market research is and how to run it across markets, from recruiting respondents to delivering incentives they can actually use.
body_markdown:
## **Quick answer**


Global market research is research conducted across multiple countries or regions to understand customers, markets, and competitors. It follows the same basic process as domestic research: recruit respondents, field the study, deliver incentives, and analyze the results. The difference is that each stage has to adapt to local languages, cultural response patterns, privacy laws, and incentive access.


## **Key takeaways**


-


Most research teams now run multi-country studies, with 88% of market and UX researchers working with global respondents.


-


Crossing borders adds complexity in language, culture, regulation, and incentive access.


-


Global studies often face operational issues like translation and incentive delivery, not just research design.


-


A smooth respondent experience, including fast and usable incentives, supports both data quality and panel retention.


You only need to look at a fast-food menu to see how consumer preferences change across borders. McDonald’s in Japan sells a[seasonal Tsukimi burger](https://japantoday.com/category/features/food/tsukimi-burgers-are-they-really-worth-the-hype) topped with a fried egg, while locations in New Zealand serve the Kiwiburger with egg and beetroot. These local offerings are a reminder that what works in one market doesn’t automatically work in another, and the same is true for research.


Most research teams already run multi-country studies. In a recent Tremendous survey,[88% of market and UX researchers said they run studies with global respondents](https://www.tremendous.com/resources/global-research-ops-playbook/) , and 42% sent incentives to 11 or more countries. But many teams still rely on tools and workflows built for single-country programs. That gap tends to show up as recruitment delays, data quality issues, and incentive headaches.


Below, you’ll find what changes when research crosses borders and how to run each stage of the respondent process, from recruitment and fieldwork to incentive delivery and re-engagement.


## **What is global market research?**


**Global market research** is the collection and analysis of data on consumer behavior, market conditions, and competitors across multiple countries or regions. Businesses use it to understand how customers in different markets think and buy, so they can tailor products, pricing, and messaging and spot new opportunities. The core challenge is comparability: Your results need to mean the same thing from one country to the next, even when respondents speak different languages and answer questions differently.


## **What changes when research crosses borders?**


Running research in multiple countries adds four layers of complexity your team needs to plan for:


**Language and translation:**[Translating a survey is more complex than translating everyday messages](https://www.surveypractice.org/article/129646-introduction-2025-special-issue-on-cross-cultural-and-multilingual-research) . Translators need to understand your subject matter, plus the idioms and culturally specific concepts that don’t carry over word for word. If a translated question reads differently than intended, your data won’t measure what you think it does.


**Cultural response patterns:**[Different cultural groups tend to answer surveys in systematic patterns](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12316043/) . Some respondents tend to agree or answer positively, known as an *acquiescent response style* . Others gravitate toward the ends of a rating scale, like “very satisfied” or “very dissatisfied,” known as an *extreme response style* .


**Data privacy and compliance:** Privacy laws including the European Union’s[General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)](https://gdpr-info.eu/) , the[Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD)](https://prod.iapp.org/resources/article/brazilian-data-protection-law-lgpd-english-translation/) , China’s[Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL)](https://en.npc.gov.cn.cdurl.cn/2021-12/29/c_694559.htm) , and Singapore’s[Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA)](https://sso.agc.gov.sg/Act/PDPA2012) set different rules for consent, data storage, and respondent rights. A privacy violation may mean you have to throw out collected data.


**Incentive access:** An incentive that works in one country can be unusable in another. Amazon has a limited presence in some regions,[PayPal isn’t supported everywhere](https://www.paypal.com/webapps/mpp/country-worldwide) , and converting currencies manually adds additional work teams often don’t plan for.

## **Global market research methods**


[Your research methods](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-market-research-survey-methodologies/) determine what type of data you collect and how you gather and analyze it. Choose based on your objective, timeline, and budget. Most global studies combine more than one method.


Method Best for Pros Cons


Qualitative (ideas, experiences, and meanings) Capturing opinions and motivations in respondents’ own words, through focus groups or interviews Flexible and works with smaller samples Harder to standardize across markets


Quantitative (numerical data) Measuring how many, how much, or how often, through surveys with multiple-choice or rating-scale questions Systematic and reproducible Needs larger samples and statistical expertise


Primary (original data from your target audience) Testing products, gauging demand, and assessing brand perception Tailored to your questions, with control over sampling Can be expensive and time-consuming


Secondary (existing studies, reports, and datasets) Spotting industry trends, sizing new markets, and analyzing competitors Often faster and less expensive No control over how the data was collected


For global studies, comparability shapes how you apply each method. For **quantitative studies** , that goes beyond accurate translation. Each question needs to measure the same thing in every region, which may mean adapting question stems, scale labels, and response options. If respondents in one market are less likely to express strong dissatisfaction, for example, test your scale labels locally before fielding. For **qualitative studies** , local moderators or interpreters can help your team catch slang, idioms, and cultural references an outside researcher might miss.


## **How to conduct global market research**


Global research moves through the same stages as domestic research: recruitment, fieldwork, incentive delivery, and re-engagement. Each one shapes the next. **Strong recruiting protects data quality, an efficient workflow keeps fieldwork moving, and a good incentive experience brings people back for your next study.**


### **1. Define objectives and prioritize markets**


Start with an objective you can measure. A goal like understanding the European market is too vague to guide a study. A goal like determining whether your pricing is competitive in Germany, France, and the Netherlands tells you exactly who to recruit and what to ask.


Studying a few markets in depth usually produces more useful insights than spreading your team thin. To choose them, review country and industry reports, economic forecasts, and consumer behavior trends. Weigh the size of your potential customer base against its growth potential, and look for barriers to entry like tariffs or regulations. A competitive analysis can also show how saturated each market is and where your product stands out.


### **2. Recruit qualified respondents in each market**


Once you’ve decided on markets, it’s time to start recruitment. Finding qualified or niche participants is the top pain point for[82% of UX researchers and 76% of market researchers](https://www.tremendous.com/resources/global-research-ops-playbook/) . Recruitment timelines and screening criteria vary by region, and mainstream panels often have[limited pools in smaller markets outside major metro areas](https://thealchemic.com/feeds/consumer-research-emerging-markets-platforms) .


[Plan your recruitment strategy](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/how-to-recruit-research-participants/) before your study launches. Evaluate whether established panel providers can reach your target population in each market. If they fall short, consider local recruitment partners and referral-based recruiting for niche profiles. To identify fraudulent or ineligible respondents,[combine screening with other quality checks](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/screener-surveys/) , such as identity verification.


No single quality-control method catches every problem.


### **3. Localize and pilot the instrument**


Word-for-word translation isn’t enough.[Choose translators carefully](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11666326/) , give them clear guidelines, and build in time for *cultural adaptation* , the step where you adjust questions so respondents in each market interpret them the same way.


Next, have bilingual researchers or local experts review the translated survey to confirm it carries the same meaning and intent as the original. For high-stakes instruments, add *back-translation* : A second translator converts the localized version back into the original language so you can compare the two and catch shifts in meaning. Once the survey is localized, pilot it with a small local sample before full fielding.


### **4. Field the study and protect data quality**


Plan for time zones when you set response windows, reminder timing, and respondent support coverage. To move faster without cutting corners, build standardized study templates you can adapt for each market, use pre-vetted panels where possible, and automate handoffs between stages.


Fraud is a growing concern in market research.[Bots, duplicate responses, and AI-generated answers increasingly compromise data quality](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/detect-ai-survey-research-responses/) , and fraud patterns can look different from one market to the next. More than[40% of market research teams lose at least 10% of their incentive budget](https://www.tremendous.com/resources/global-research-ops-playbook/) to fraud.


Build a layered defense instead of relying on one check. Verify identities at recruitment, monitor respondent behavior during fielding,[run fraud checks before incentives go out](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/research-fraud-signals-incentive-platforms/) , and clean your data after collection. Don’t rely on post-collection cleaning as your main safeguard. By that point, incentives have usually already gone out.


### **5. Deliver incentives respondents can actually use**


Incentives are often the last thing teams plan for operationally and one of the first things to break. A respondent might finish your survey, then receive a gift card for a retailer that doesn’t operate in their country. Or they might wait a week for an incentive in a currency they can’t easily use. That friction undercuts the motivation the incentive was meant to create.


The effects add up. A poor incentive experience can lower completion rates, leave incentives unredeemed, and make respondents less likely to join your next study. In Tremendous’ Global Research Ops Playbook for 2026,[currency conversion was the top global incentive challenge for 62% of market research firms](https://www.tremendous.com/resources/global-research-ops-playbook/) , followed by local reward availability (58%) and tax and regulatory compliance (50%).


**For global respondents, a usable incentive comes down to a few basics:**


-


**Local currency:** Respondents receive their incentive in the currency they use every day.


-


**Familiar options:** They can choose local gift card brands or monetary options like PayPal, where supported.


-


**Their own language:** Delivery emails and redemption instructions appear in the respondent’s language.


-


**Fast delivery:** Incentives arrive promptly after the study ends.


Meeting those expectations market by market gets complicated when you’re juggling separate vendors, catalogs, and per-country workflows.


Partnering with a[global incentive platform with an international catalog, like Tremendous](https://www.tremendous.com/solutions/market-research/) , simplifies the process. You can send incentives to every market from one place, track spend in one dashboard, and give respondents options that work where they live. Look for one that[handles local currencies and languages](https://www.tremendous.com/products/global-payouts/) for you and includes fraud checks before incentives go out.


### **6. Analyze within and across markets**


Analyze each market on its own terms first, accounting for the cultural response patterns you identified earlier. A score that looks low in one country may just reflect how respondents there use rating scales.


Then compare markets side by side. The similarities and differences between regions are often the most valuable finding, since they show where one strategy can work globally and where you’ll need to adapt.


Map your findings back to your original objective. Decision-oriented research, like demand validation or product-market fit studies, should end in a clear recommendation on whether to move forward. Exploratory research, like customer attitude studies, usually summarizes what you learned and highlights meaningful differences between markets.


### **7. Re-engage respondents for future studies**


Keeping respondents engaged usually[costs less than recruiting new ones](https://www.tremendous.com/blog/incentives-research-panel-quality/) for every study. That matters even more in new markets, where trust takes time to build.


A smooth first experience is what earns a second one: a clear research instrument, a prompt and usable incentive, and responsive support. From there, localize your follow-up cadence and thank-you messages for each market, and deliver incentives consistently from study to study. You’ll also need the right consent to store respondent data and re-contact people under each market’s privacy laws.


## **How to succeed in global market research**


Global research works when you plan for differences in language, culture, regulation, and incentive access in every market you study, then design each stage of the process around them. **Incentives are one piece of that process, but they shape whether people participate, finish your study, and come back for the next one** . Adapt recruitment, fieldwork, incentives, and follow-up to each market, and you’re more likely to collect reliable insights you can compare across borders.
